---
title: "Toyota vs Subaru Warranties"
subtitle: "bZ4X Touring and e-Outback: identical hardware, near-identical mechanism, one number apart"
date: "`r format(Sys.Date(), '%d %B %Y')`"
output:
  html_document:
    theme: flatly
    toc: true
    toc_float: true
    toc_depth: 3
params:
  # --- contract terms (facts, not estimates) ---
  base_km: 160000
  base_years: 8
  age_ceiling: 10
  increment_km: 15000
  toyota_ceiling_km: 1000000
  subaru_ceiling_km: 200000
  subaru_no_grant_km: 185000
  soh_threshold: 0.70

  # --- degradation calibration A (benign) ---
  cal_a_calendar_loss_10y: 6
  cal_a_km_crit_pure: 600000
  cal_a_sd_unit: 0.22

  # --- degradation calibration B (adverse) ---
  cal_b_calendar_loss_10y: 10
  cal_b_km_crit_pure: 450000
  cal_b_sd_unit: 0.25

  # --- usage rate distribution ---
  med_rate: 15000
  sdlog_rate: 0.6

  # --- financial (ALL REAL, today's DKK) ---
  # Severity is two different numbers depending on who is paying. Sections 6
  # and 8 need what it costs the manufacturer to honour a claim; section 7
  # needs what the buyer would pay if NOT covered, at retail and including
  # Danish VAT. Both are UNSOURCED assumptions - see section 1.2.
  severity_maker_dkk: 67000
  severity_buyer_dkk: 100000
  severity_buyer_sensitivity: [67000, 100000, 150000, 200000]
  severity_decline: 0.08
  discount_real: 0.02
  repair_worthy: 0.75

  # --- persistency ---
  pi_check: 1.0
  pi_sensitivity: [1.0, 0.98, 0.95]
  # Toyota DK's terms indicate a missed check suspends rather than destroys
  # cover, so "reinstatable" is the default. "permanent" is the older reading,
  # shown alongside because the two differ by more than an order of magnitude.
  lapse_mode: reinstatable

  # --- service economics ---
  # Full per-visit prices, not premiums. Services alternate: a small one at odd
  # multiples of the interval, a large one at even multiples.
  #
  # TOYOTA: SOURCED. Toyota Koege price calculator, retrieved 2 September 2026.
  # https://www.toyota-koege.dk/vaerksted/kalkulator
  service_toyota_small_dkk: 2495
  service_toyota_large_dkk: 3495
  toyota_prices_sourced: TRUE

  # SUBARU: SOURCED. Written quote from an authorised Subaru workshop in
  # Denmark, 3 September 2026, for an e-Outback 280 kW, incl. VAT. (The
  # workshop is not named here: the quote was issued to an individual, not
  # published as a tariff.) Same alternating pattern as Toyota: small at odd
  # multiples, large at even.
  # The quote runs only to 75,000 km / 5 years; beyond that, prices are held
  # flat, which is an extrapolation - see section 7.4.
  service_subaru_small_dkk: 2411.25
  service_subaru_large_dkk: 3366.53
  subaru_prices_sourced: TRUE
  subaru_quoted_to_km: 75000

  # INDEPENDENT: PLACEHOLDER, no quote obtained. Now the binding unknown -
  # see section 7.5, which inverts the question to ask what it would have to be.
  service_independent_small_dkk: 1600
  service_independent_large_dkk: 2200
  independent_prices_sourced: FALSE
  independent_sensitivity: [1200, 1600, 2000, 2400]

  service_margin_low: 500
  service_margin_high: 1500

  # --- servicing strategy ---
  # 0 = franchised dealer from new. Because cover is reinstatable (3.3), a
  # buyer can use an independent early and return to the dealer later.
  dealer_from_year: 0
  dealer_from_grid: [0, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8]

  # --- travel to the workshop, round trip per visit ---
  # Only DIFFERENCES matter, so only differences need entering. Both are
  # measured against your Subaru dealer; negative means nearer than it.
  travel_extra_toyota_km: 40
  travel_extra_independent_km: 0
  # Marginal cost per km: energy, tyres and wear, plus whatever the driver
  # puts on their own time. UNSOURCED judgement - see section 1.1.
  travel_cost_dkk_per_km: 2.5
  travel_cost_sensitivity: [1.0, 2.5, 4.0]

  # --- the buyer's own situation (set these before knitting) ---
  my_rate: 30000             # km/yr you actually expect to drive
  my_rate_compare: 20000     # a second rate to compare against, e.g. the kink
  my_holding_years: 10       # years you expect to keep the car
  my_dealer_anyway: TRUE     # would you use a franchised dealer regardless?
  my_price_gap_dkk: 0        # how much more the Toyota costs to buy, if any

  # --- resale of unused cover ---
  # Share of the actuarial value of remaining warranty that a used-car buyer
  # actually pays for. The least well grounded number in the note; see 7.6.
  resale_capitalisation: 0.6
  resale_cap_sensitivity: [0.3, 0.6, 1.0]
  holding_grid: [3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10]

  # --- presentation ---
  buyer_rates: [15000, 20000, 25000, 40000, 60000]
  cap_grid: [160000, 200000, 300000, 400000, 500000, 650000, 1000000]
  discount_sensitivity: [0.01, 0.02, 0.05]
  # Genuinely credible range for the real rate. The 5% in the grid above is
  # carried only to demonstrate insensitivity, not as a defensible value.
  discount_credible: [0.01, 0.02]
  decline_sensitivity: [0.03, 0.06, 0.08, 0.10, 0.12]
  ref_rate: 40000
  fx_dkk_eur: 7.46

  # --- optional Monte Carlo cross-check ---
  use_simulation: FALSE
  n_sim: 1000000
  seed: 101

```{r derived, include=FALSE}
num <- \(x) as.numeric(unlist(x))

d_crit <- 100 * (1 - params$soh_threshold)

cal <- list(
  A = c(
    deg_coefs(params$cal_a_calendar_loss_10y, params$cal_a_km_crit_pure, d_crit),
    list(
      sd_unit = params$cal_a_sd_unit,
      calendar_loss_10y = params$cal_a_calendar_loss_10y,
      km_crit_pure = params$cal_a_km_crit_pure,
      label = "A (benign)"
    )
  ),
  B = c(
    deg_coefs(params$cal_b_calendar_loss_10y, params$cal_b_km_crit_pure, d_crit),
    list(
      sd_unit = params$cal_b_sd_unit,
      calendar_loss_10y = params$cal_b_calendar_loss_10y,
      km_crit_pure = params$cal_b_km_crit_pure,
      label = "B (adverse)"
    )
  )
)

buyer_rates <- num(params$buyer_rates)
cap_grid <- num(params$cap_grid)
discount_grid <- num(params$discount_sensitivity)
discount_cred <- num(params$discount_credible)
decline_grid <- num(params$decline_sensitivity)
pi_grid <- num(params$pi_sensitivity)

# Partial application so the call sites stay readable.
rate_of <- function(cc, years, cap_km, pi_check = 1,
                    lapse_mode = params$lapse_mode) {
  claim_rate(
    years, cap_km, cc$a, cc$b, cc$sd_unit, d_crit,
    params$med_rate, params$sdlog_rate, pi_check,
    params$base_km, params$increment_km, lapse_mode
  )
}

gap_of <- function(cc, rate, discount = params$discount_real,
                   decline = params$severity_decline,
                   severity = params$severity_buyer_dkk,
                   dealer_from = params$dealer_from_year) {
  gap_value(
    rate, cc$a, cc$b, cc$sd_unit, d_crit,
    params$age_ceiling, params$toyota_ceiling_km, params$subaru_ceiling_km,
    severity, decline, discount, params$repair_worthy,
    cover_from = dealer_from
  )
}

# Small/large price pair per network. The alternation is a real feature of the
# published Toyota tariff, not a modelling convenience.
price_set <- function(ind_small = params$service_independent_small_dkk,
                      ind_large = params$service_independent_large_dkk,
                      per_km = params$travel_cost_dkk_per_km) {
  # Getting there is part of the price of a visit, and the three destinations
  # are not equidistant. Only differences matter, so a common component would
  # cancel; what does not cancel is the extra distance to the Toyota dealer.
  trav <- function(km) km * per_km

  # The Subaru dealer is the baseline, so it carries no travel term; any
  # component common to all three would cancel out of the difference anyway.
  list(
    toyota = c(params$service_toyota_small_dkk, params$service_toyota_large_dkk) +
      trav(params$travel_extra_toyota_km),
    subaru = c(params$service_subaru_small_dkk, params$service_subaru_large_dkk),
    independent = c(ind_small, ind_large) +
      trav(params$travel_extra_independent_km)
  )
}

travel_extra_toyota_km <- params$travel_extra_toyota_km

# Ratio of large to small, used to scale an independent quote given as one
# number into a consistent pair.
ind_ratio <- params$service_independent_large_dkk /
  params$service_independent_small_dkk

# Subaru counts as still-placeholder only while it is both unsourced and
# identical to Toyota; supplying figures should switch the prose over.
subaru_placeholder <- !isTRUE(params$subaru_prices_sourced) &&
  identical(
    c(params$service_subaru_small_dkk, params$service_subaru_large_dkk),
    c(params$service_toyota_small_dkk, params$service_toyota_large_dkk)
  )

# `dealer_anyway` is a scenario, not a setting: the note reports both
# throughout rather than picking one, because it is the single largest swing
# factor in the buyer's answer and only the buyer knows which applies.
cost_of <- function(rate, dealer_anyway = FALSE,
                    discount = params$discount_real,
                    prices = price_set(),
                    horizon = Inf,
                    dealer_from = params$dealer_from_year) {
  servicing_differential(
    rate, params$age_ceiling, params$subaru_ceiling_km, params$increment_km,
    prices, discount, horizon_years = horizon,
    dealer_anyway = dealer_anyway, dealer_from = dealer_from
  )
}

# Mean cost of a visit under the alternating schedule, for prose.
mean_visit <- function(pair) mean(pair)

scenarios <- tibble(
  dealer_anyway = c(FALSE, TRUE),
  scenario = c("Independent workshop otherwise", "Franchised dealer regardless")
)

# Formatting helpers
fmt_km  <- \(x) formatC(x, format = "d", big.mark = ",")
fmt_dkk <- \(x) formatC(round(x), format = "d", big.mark = ",")
fmt_pct <- \(x, dp = 2) paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = dp), "%")
fmt_num <- \(x, dp = 1) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = dp)

show_table <- function(x, ...) {
  kable(x, ...) |>
    kable_styling(full_width = FALSE, position = "left",
                  bootstrap_options = c("striped", "condensed"))
}
```

```{r headline-numbers, include=FALSE}
uncapped <- map_dbl(cal, \(cc) rate_of(cc, params$age_ceiling, Inf))

checks_to_toyota <- checks_required(
  params$toyota_ceiling_km, params$base_km, params$increment_km, from_zero = TRUE
)
checks_to_subaru <- checks_required(
  params$subaru_ceiling_km, params$base_km, params$increment_km, from_zero = TRUE
)
extra_to_toyota <- checks_required(
  params$toyota_ceiling_km, params$base_km, params$increment_km
)
extra_to_subaru <- checks_required(
  params$subaru_ceiling_km, params$base_km, params$increment_km
)

# Usage rate below which the two contracts coincide: cap / T
gap_opens_at <- params$subaru_ceiling_km / params$age_ceiling

buyer_gap <- expand_grid(rate = buyer_rates, calib = names(cal)) |>
  mutate(res = map2(calib, rate, \(k, r) gap_of(cal[[k]], r))) |>
  unnest(res, names_repair = "unique") |>
  select(rate = rate...1, calib, term_subaru, term_toyota, p_gap, t_bar, pv_dkk)

pv_at <- function(r, k) {
  buyer_gap |>
    filter(rate == r, calib == k) |>
    pull(pv_dkk)
}
```

```{r buyer-case, include=FALSE}
# Everything specific to the reader's own situation, computed once so the
# verdict can be stated up front and the working shown later.
stopifnot(
  "my_rate must be positive" = params$my_rate > 0,
  "my_holding_years must be positive" = params$my_holding_years > 0,
  "my_dealer_anyway must be TRUE or FALSE" = is.logical(params$my_dealer_anyway)
)

my <- list(
  rate = params$my_rate,
  hold = params$my_holding_years,
  dealer = isTRUE(params$my_dealer_anyway),
  price_gap = params$my_price_gap_dkk
)

my$binds <- my$rate > gap_opens_at
my$term_subaru <- warranty_term(my$rate, params$age_ceiling,
                                params$subaru_ceiling_km)
my$term_toyota <- warranty_term(my$rate, params$age_ceiling,
                                params$toyota_ceiling_km)

# Gap value over the full contract, and over the buyer's own holding period.
my$gap_full <- map_dbl(names(cal), \(k) gap_of(cal[[k]], my$rate)$pv_dkk) |>
  set_names(names(cal))

my$gap_held <- map_dbl(names(cal), \(k) gap_value(
  my$rate, cal[[k]]$a, cal[[k]]$b, cal[[k]]$sd_unit, d_crit,
  params$age_ceiling, params$toyota_ceiling_km, params$subaru_ceiling_km,
  params$severity_buyer_dkk, params$severity_decline, params$discount_real,
  params$repair_worthy, horizon_years = my$hold
)$pv_dkk) |>
  set_names(names(cal))

my$gap_transferred <- my$gap_full - my$gap_held

# --- holding period ---------------------------------------------------------
cap_default <- params$resale_capitalisation
# NB: distinct from cap_grid, which holds the mileage ceilings.
cap_share_grid <- num(params$resale_cap_sensitivity)
hold_grid <- sort(unique(c(num(params$holding_grid), params$my_holding_years)))
hold_grid <- hold_grid[hold_grid > 0 & hold_grid <= params$age_ceiling]

hold_value <- function(k, sale_year, capitalisation = cap_default,
                       dealer_anyway = my$dealer) {
  holding_value(
    my$rate, cal[[k]]$a, cal[[k]]$b, cal[[k]]$sd_unit, d_crit,
    params$age_ceiling, params$toyota_ceiling_km, params$subaru_ceiling_km,
    params$severity_buyer_dkk, params$severity_decline, params$discount_real,
    params$repair_worthy, sale_year, params$increment_km,
    price_set(), capitalisation,
    dealer_anyway = dealer_anyway
  ) |>
    mutate(calib = k, capitalisation = capitalisation)
}

holding_tbl <- expand_grid(calib = names(cal), sale_year = hold_grid) |>
  pmap(\(calib, sale_year) hold_value(calib, sale_year)) |>
  list_rbind()

my$hold_now <- holding_tbl |> filter(sale_year == my$hold)
my$hold_best <- holding_tbl |>
  group_by(calib) |>
  slice_max(net_pv, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ungroup()
my$hold_optimal <- all(abs(my$hold_best$sale_year - my$hold) < 1e-9)

# Both servicing scenarios are carried through; `my$dealer` only says which one
# the buyer expects to be in, it does not suppress the other.
my$cost <- c(
  independent = cost_of(my$rate, dealer_anyway = FALSE)$pv_dkk,
  dealer = cost_of(my$rate, dealer_anyway = TRUE)$pv_dkk
)
my$cost_faced <- if (my$dealer) my$cost[["dealer"]] else my$cost[["independent"]]
my$cost_full <- my$cost[["independent"]]
my$visits <- cost_of(my$rate, dealer_anyway = FALSE)
my$extra_visits <- my$visits$visits_freed

my$net <- my$gap_full - my$cost_faced
my$net_both <- list(
  independent = my$gap_full - my$cost[["independent"]],
  dealer = my$gap_full - my$cost[["dealer"]]
)
# With the Toyota tariff now known, the live inversion is the independent
# price: above it the ceiling pays, below it the independent wins.
my$be_ind <- map_dbl(names(cal), \(k) breakeven_independent(
  my$gap_full[[k]], my$rate, params$age_ceiling, params$subaru_ceiling_km,
  params$increment_km, price_set(), params$discount_real,
  dealer_anyway = my$dealer
)) |>
  set_names(names(cal))

# The most the mileage ceiling alone can justify paying at purchase.
my$worth <- range(my$net)

my$verdict <- if (!my$binds) {
  "identical"
} else if (max(my$net) <= 0) {
  "does not clear"
} else if (min(my$net) > 0) {
  "clears"
} else {
  "clears only on the adverse calibration"
}

rng <- function(x, f = fmt_dkk) {
  lo <- min(x)
  hi <- max(x)
  if (isTRUE(all.equal(lo, hi))) return(f(lo))
  # A dash joiner is unreadable when either end is negative: "-3,320-2,387"
  # reads as a range spanning zero rather than one lying wholly below it.
  paste0(f(lo), if (lo < 0) " to " else "–", f(hi))
}
```

Working note, `r format(Sys.Date(), '%d %B %Y')`. Currency: DKK, **all figures real in today's money**. Toyota's Danish terms and service tariff are sourced directly; Subaru's Danish terms are still taken from the Nordic release (section 1.1).

> **How to read this.** The document is generated from the parameter block in its source; every number below is computed at knit time, so changing an assumption and re-knitting updates the tables and the prose together. Section 1.1 sets out where the numbers come from and which are unsourced, section 1.2 the financial framing, section 3 the actuarial machinery, and sections 6 and 7 the two questions that actually differ — what the contract costs the manufacturer across a whole fleet, and what it is worth to one buyer. Terminology specific to insurance is glossed where it first appears.
>
> **If you are choosing between the two cars**, set `my_rate`, `my_holding_years`, `my_dealer_anyway`, `dealer_from_year` and the three round-trip distances in the parameter block, then read section 7.8. The verdict for the values currently set is immediately below. Section 9 covers what to do with these numbers in a negotiation.

## Your inputs

Everything below is computed from these. They are the only values a reader needs to change; the rest of the parameter block holds contract terms and sourced prices.

## The answer, for the usage currently set

```{r answer-box, results='asis'}
bullets <- c()

if (!my$binds) {
  bullets <- c(bullets, paste0(
    "**At ", fmt_km(my$rate), " km/yr the two battery warranties are identical.** ",
    "You would need to drive more than ", fmt_km(gap_opens_at),
    " km/yr before Subaru's mileage ceiling binds inside the ",
    params$age_ceiling, "-year age limit. The difference is not small; it is ",
    "exactly zero, and no financial assumption changes that. Decide on other grounds."
  ))
} else {
  bullets <- c(bullets, paste0(
    "**Gross value of Toyota's higher ceiling to you: ", rng(my$gap_full),
    " DKK.** Your Subaru cover would end at year ",
    fmt_num(my$term_subaru), "; the Toyota runs to year ",
    fmt_num(my$term_toyota), ". The range spans the two degradation scenarios, ",
    "which is the dominant uncertainty."
  ))

  # Both servicing scenarios are always shown; the buyer's stated expectation
  # is marked rather than used to hide the other.
  bullets <- c(bullets, paste0(
    "**Servicing splits the answer in two, and it is the largest swing factor.**",
    " If you would otherwise use an independent workshop, holding the cover ",
    "costs you ", fmt_dkk(my$cost[["independent"]]), " DKK (",
    fmt_num(my$extra_visits, 0), " extra visits tied to a Toyota dealer), leaving ",
    rng(my$net_both$independent), " DKK. If you would use a franchised dealer ",
    "regardless, the cost is ", fmt_dkk(my$cost[["dealer"]]),
    " DKK — both owners then service at a dealer throughout, so what bites is ",
    "the difference in the two tariffs plus the ",
    fmt_km(travel_extra_toyota_km), " km of extra driving to the Toyota ",
    "workshop each visit",
    if (subaru_placeholder) ", and with the tariffs set equal it is currently all travel"
    else "",
    " — leaving ", rng(my$net_both$dealer), " DKK. ",
    "You have said **", if (my$dealer) "the franchised-dealer case" else
      "the independent-workshop case", "** applies to you."
  ))

  bullets <- c(bullets, paste0(
    "**Verdict on your stated case: the mileage ceiling ", my$verdict, ".** ",
    if (my$dealer && subaru_placeholder) paste0(
      "In this scenario the answer turns on Toyota's tariff against Subaru's, ",
      "and Subaru's is not yet known — the two are currently set equal, which ",
      "is a placeholder and not a finding. "
    ) else if (my$dealer) paste0(
      "In this scenario the answer turns on the two franchised tariffs: Toyota ",
      "at ", fmt_dkk(params$service_toyota_small_dkk), "/",
      fmt_dkk(params$service_toyota_large_dkk), " DKK against Subaru at ",
      fmt_dkk(params$service_subaru_small_dkk), "/",
      fmt_dkk(params$service_subaru_large_dkk), " DKK a visit, worth ",
      fmt_dkk(my$cost[["dealer"]]), " DKK over the term. "
    ) else if (is.finite(max(my$be_ind))) paste0(
      "It would clear if an independent workshop charged more than ",
      rng(my$be_ind), " DKK for a small service (scaling the large one in ",
      "proportion) — i.e. the ceiling pays only when servicing elsewhere is ",
      "*not* much cheaper than Toyota's ",
      fmt_dkk(params$service_toyota_small_dkk), " DKK. "
    ) else "",
    "Toyota's prices are sourced; ",
    if (subaru_placeholder) "Subaru's and the independent's are not"
    else "the independent's is not",
    " (section 1.1)."
  ))

  bullets <- c(bullets, paste0(
    "**You do not have to commit for ten years.** Cover is reinstatable and the ",
    "base guarantee runs unconditionally to year ",
    fmt_num(params$base_km / my$rate),
    ", so servicing elsewhere until Subaru's ceiling falls in year ",
    fmt_num(my$term_subaru),
    " and only then returning to Toyota keeps the whole gap value while cutting ",
    "your Toyota visits sharply. Section 7.10 prices it."
  ))

  bullets <- c(bullets, if (max(my$gap_transferred) < 1) paste0(
    "**Selling in year ", fmt_num(my$hold, 0),
    " means you capture all of it as claims**, since your cover would run out ",
    "in year ", fmt_num(my$term_toyota),
    " anyway. Holding to the end is the value-maximising choice, and selling ",
    "earlier hands part of the cover to the next owner at a discount ",
    "(section 7.6)."
  ) else paste0(
    "**Only ", rng(my$gap_held),
    " DKK of that falls while you still own the car**, over your ",
    fmt_num(my$hold, 0), " years of ownership. The remaining ",
    rng(my$gap_transferred),
    " DKK is cover you hand on; you recover roughly ",
    fmt_pct(cap_default, 0),
    " of it in the resale price, which is why holding longer is worth more ",
    "(section 7.6)."
  ))
}

if (my$price_gap > 0) {
  # max(my$worth) is the most generous reading: net value on the adverse fade
  # scenario, which is the upper end of the calibration bracket.
  best <- max(my$worth)

  bullets <- c(bullets, if (best >= my$price_gap) paste0(
    "**On price:** at ", fmt_dkk(my$price_gap),
    " DKK the Toyota's premium is covered by the warranty difference alone, ",
    "which is worth up to ", fmt_dkk(best),
    " DKK to you on the adverse fade scenario. On this dimension it is not ",
    "overpriced — though that is the *most* generous reading, and the benign ",
    "scenario gives only ", fmt_dkk(min(my$worth)), " DKK."
  ) else paste0(
    "**On price:** the battery warranty alone justifies at most ",
    fmt_dkk(max(0, best)), " DKK of the ", fmt_dkk(my$price_gap),
    " DKK you say the Toyota costs more, and that is on the adverse fade ",
    "scenario. The other ", fmt_dkk(my$price_gap - max(0, best)),
    " DKK has to be justified by something this note does not model."
  ))
}

cat(paste0("- ", bullets, collapse = "\n"))
```

*Set `my_rate` and the other `my_*` parameters to your own situation and re-knit. Section 7.8 shows the working, and section 11 the caveats that could overturn it.*

---

## 1. Scope and assumptions

The two vehicles are the same car: shared e-TNGA platform, same cells, same pack, same BMS, same thermal management. This makes the comparison an unusually clean natural experiment — the engineering substrate is held constant and only the contract varies.

```{r assumptions}
tibble(
  Parameter = c(
    "Capacity threshold",
    "Pack replacement severity (maker)",
    "Pack replacement severity (buyer)",
    "Severity decline",
    "Discount rate",
    "Repair-worthiness factor",
    "Usage rate distribution",
    "FX"
  ),
  Value = c(
    paste0(fmt_pct(params$soh_threshold, 0), " of original"),
    paste0(fmt_dkk(params$severity_maker_dkk), " DKK"),
    paste0(fmt_dkk(params$severity_buyer_dkk), " DKK"),
    paste0(fmt_pct(params$severity_decline, 0), "/yr real"),
    paste0(fmt_pct(params$discount_real, 0), " real"),
    fmt_num(params$repair_worthy, 2),
    paste0("lognormal, median ", fmt_km(params$med_rate),
           " km/yr, sigma_log = ", params$sdlog_rate),
    paste0(fmt_num(params$fx_dkk_eur, 2), " DKK/EUR")
  ),
  Basis = c(
    "Both contracts",
    paste0("Unsourced; ~EUR ", fmt_dkk(params$severity_maker_dkk / params$fx_dkk_eur),
           ". Cost to the maker of honouring a claim"),
    "Unsourced; retail incl. VAT if NOT covered. See section 1.1",
    "Falling pack prices",
    "See section 1.2",
    "P(vehicle still economic to repair at claim)",
    "Assumption, roughly European private-car",
    "Peg central rate"
  )
) |>
  show_table(align = "lll")
```

**Verification status.** **Toyota's Danish terms have now been read directly** (toyota.dk, retrieved 2 September 2026; Appendix C) and they confirm the structure assumed throughout: a capacity guarantee of `r params$base_years` yr / `r fmt_km(params$base_km)` km at `r fmt_pct(params$soh_threshold, 0)`, extended by one year *or* `r fmt_km(params$increment_km)` km — *"hvad der kommer først"* — per EV health check at an authorised Toyota workshop, up to *"`r params$age_ceiling` år eller `r fmt_km(params$toyota_ceiling_km)` km"*, and transferable: *"Alle standardgarantier overføres til en evt. ny ejer."* The dealer tie on which the whole servicing argument rests is real, and so is the transferability the resale channel in section 7.6 depends on.

Subaru's Nordic terms are confirmed from the Subaru Norge press release of 16 January 2026, but **Subaru's Danish terms have still not been read**, and neither has their service tariff. The asymmetry in what is verified now runs the other way from before.

### 1.1 Where these numbers come from

Toyota's Danish contract terms and service tariff are sourced directly, as is Subaru's service tariff. **Several financial inputs are not**, and it is worth being blunt about which is which, because the ones still missing are exactly the ones the buyer's answer turns on.

```{r provenance}
tibble(
  Input = c(
    "Warranty terms, both makes",
    "Capacity threshold and increment rule",
    "Usage rate distribution",
    "Pack replacement severity",
    "Toyota service tariff (DK)",
    "Subaru service tariff (DK)",
    "Independent workshop price",
    "Dealer gross margin per visit",
    "Severity decline",
    "Repair-worthiness factor",
    "Real discount rate",
    "Degradation calibration"
  ),
  Status = c(
    "**Sourced**", "**Sourced**", "Assumption", "**Unsourced**", "**Sourced**",
    "**Sourced**", "**Unsourced**", "**Unsourced**", "Assumption", "Assumption",
    "Sourced (market)", "Bracketed"
  ),
  Basis = c(
    "Toyota DK read directly (2 Sep 2026); Subaru still on the Norwegian release",
    "Confirmed for Toyota DK; Subaru assumed to carry from Norway",
    "Lognormal, median assumed, roughly European private-car",
    paste0(fmt_dkk(params$severity_maker_dkk), " DKK stated as ~EUR ",
           fmt_dkk(params$severity_maker_dkk / params$fx_dkk_eur),
           "; no price quoted, perspective unstated"),
    paste0(fmt_dkk(params$service_toyota_small_dkk), " / ",
           fmt_dkk(params$service_toyota_large_dkk),
           " DKK, alternating. Toyota Koege calculator, retrieved 2 Sep 2026"),
    paste0(fmt_num(params$service_subaru_small_dkk, 2), " / ",
           fmt_num(params$service_subaru_large_dkk, 2),
           " DKK. Authorised Subaru workshop quote, 3 Sep 2026; only to ",
           fmt_km(params$subaru_quoted_to_km), " km"),
    paste0("No quote obtained. Placeholder ",
           fmt_dkk(params$service_independent_small_dkk), " / ",
           fmt_dkk(params$service_independent_large_dkk), " DKK; see section 7.5"),
    paste0(fmt_dkk(params$service_margin_low), "-",
           fmt_dkk(params$service_margin_high), " DKK; an informed guess"),
    "Falling pack prices; direction well established, rate is not",
    "Judgement; not estimated from data",
    "Danish 10Y less anchored inflation expectations (section 1.2)",
    "Two scenarios chosen to bracket, not one estimate"
  )
) |>
  show_table(align = "lll")
```

Two of these deserve more than a row.

**Pack replacement severity, and whose cost it is.** The `r fmt_dkk(params$severity_maker_dkk)` DKK figure carries no price quotation behind it; the "~EUR `r fmt_dkk(params$severity_maker_dkk / params$fx_dkk_eur)`" is a restatement of the same number, not a source for it. Worse, it was originally used for two different quantities that cannot be the same number:

- **What it costs the manufacturer** to honour a claim — cells and labour at their own cost. This is what sections 6 and 8 need, since they price the manufacturer's liability.
- **What it costs the buyer** if the claim falls *outside* cover — a retail pack, retail labour, and Danish VAT on both. This is what section 7 needs, since that is the loss the warranty protects against.

The second is materially larger than the first, so they are carried as separate parameters: `severity_maker_dkk` at `r fmt_dkk(params$severity_maker_dkk)` DKK and `severity_buyer_dkk` at `r fmt_dkk(params$severity_buyer_dkk)`.

Neither is quoted, and the buyer-side figure deserves its reasoning set out, because **the verdict now turns on it more than on anything else**. Three considerations pull in different directions:

- **A new pack at Danish retail is dear.** Plausibly `r fmt_dkk(150000)` DKK before labour, and VAT sits on top of both. That argues for a figure well above the trade cost.
- **But the guarantee does not deliver a new pack.** Toyota's obligation is to restore capacity to *above* `r fmt_pct(params$soh_threshold, 0)`, not to as-new. A remanufactured pack that merely clears the threshold discharges it. So what the cover is worth to the buyer is the cost of getting back over the line, which need not be a full retail replacement — and by the same token the maker's cost is lower again.
- **And the claim, if it comes, is years away.** At `r fmt_km(my$rate)` km/yr the mean crossing inside the gap window falls in year `r fmt_num(buyer_gap$t_bar[buyer_gap$rate == my$rate & buyer_gap$calib == "B"], 1)`. Applying the `r fmt_pct(params$severity_decline, 0)` real decline, a pack costing X today costs about `r fmt_pct(0.92^buyer_gap$t_bar[buyer_gap$rate == my$rate & buyer_gap$calib == "B"], 0)` of X by then. The decline assumption is doing as much work as the level.

`r fmt_dkk(params$severity_buyer_dkk)` DKK is a deliberate middle: above the trade figure, below a full retail replacement, on the reasoning that restoring to threshold costs less than fitting new. Section 7.9 brackets it from `r fmt_dkk(min(num(params$severity_buyer_sensitivity)))` to `r fmt_dkk(max(num(params$severity_buyer_sensitivity)))` DKK and gives the level at which the verdict turns. **A written quote from a Danish dealer for an out-of-warranty replacement would settle the single most load-bearing number in the note** — and it is worth asking specifically what they would fit: a new pack, or a reconditioned one to threshold.

**Service pricing.** Toyota's Danish tariff is sourced from the Toyota Køge price calculator (retrieved 2 September 2026): `r fmt_dkk(params$service_toyota_small_dkk)` DKK for a *lille service* at odd multiples of the `r fmt_km(params$increment_km)` km interval and `r fmt_dkk(params$service_toyota_large_dkk)` DKK for a *stort service* at even multiples, so an owner alternates. The model enumerates those visits individually, at their own prices, rather than working from an average.

**Subaru's tariff is sourced from a dealer quote of 3 September 2026** — `r fmt_num(params$service_subaru_small_dkk, 2)` / `r fmt_num(params$service_subaru_large_dkk, 2)` DKK on the same alternating pattern — with one important limitation: it runs only to `r fmt_km(params$subaru_quoted_to_km)` km, which at the buyer's mileage is the first five of twenty visits. Section 7.4 shows how much of the answer rests on extrapolating the rest, and how little it would take to overturn it.

**No independent quote has been obtained**, which remains the binding unknown for the other scenario. Section 7.5 inverts the question and reports what an independent would have to charge for the answer to change, converting the remaining guess into a threshold a single phone call can test.

### 1.2 The discount rate, and the direction of the risk adjustment

**Severity** — the insurance term for the size of a single claim once one occurs, as against **frequency**, the probability that one occurs at all — is stated here in today's DKK and declines at `r fmt_pct(params$severity_decline, 0)` **real** per year as pack prices fall. The cash flow being discounted is therefore real, and the discount rate must be real to match. Applying a nominal rate to it would deflate the flow twice.

Danish 10-year government yields were around 3.0–3.1% nominal in mid-August 2026 (52-week range roughly 2.41–3.12%). With long-run inflation expectations anchored near 2%, that implies a real 10-year rate near **1.0%**. The default of `r fmt_pct(params$discount_real, 0)` real used here is therefore deliberately conservative; `r fmt_pct(min(discount_grid), 0)` is closer to market-implied. Both are shown throughout.

The second point concerns the *direction* of the risk adjustment, which is easy to get backwards here. This is an insurance payoff accruing to a single, undiversified household. The correct treatment of an undiversifiable, lumpy, five-figure tail is **a low (near risk-free) discount rate plus a positive risk loading on the expected value** — a **risk loading** being the margin an insurer adds above the expected claim cost as the price of bearing variance, and the same margin a risk-averse buyer should be willing to pay to shed it. Reaching for an elevated discount rate instead gets the sign wrong: raising the discount rate *reduces* the computed value of protection against a risk the buyer cannot pool, which is the opposite of what risk aversion implies. Every PV below is an expected value with no loading applied, and is therefore a **lower bound** on what a risk-averse buyer should be willing to pay.

---

## 2. The two contracts

```{r contracts}
tibble(
  ` ` = c(
    "Base battery guarantee", "Increment per health check", "Capacity threshold",
    "Age ceiling", "Mileage ceiling", "Further limit", "Transferable"
  ),
  Toyota = c(
    paste0(params$base_years, " yr / ", fmt_km(params$base_km), " km"),
    paste0("1 yr **or ", fmt_km(params$increment_km), " km**, whichever first"),
    fmt_pct(params$soh_threshold, 0),
    paste0(params$age_ceiling, " yr"),
    paste0("**", fmt_km(params$toyota_ceiling_km), " km**"),
    "—",
    "Yes"
  ),
  `Subaru (Nordic, MY2026+)` = c(
    paste0(params$base_years, " yr / ", fmt_km(params$base_km), " km"),
    paste0("1 yr **or ", fmt_km(params$increment_km), " km**, whichever first"),
    fmt_pct(params$soh_threshold, 0),
    paste0(params$age_ceiling, " yr"),
    paste0("**", fmt_km(params$subaru_ceiling_km), " km**"),
    paste0("No extension granted past ", fmt_km(params$subaru_no_grant_km), " km"),
    "Yes — follows the car"
  )
) |>
  show_table(align = "lll")
```

The mechanisms are structurally identical. Same base, same accrual rule, same threshold, same age ceiling. **One number differs**, by a factor of `r fmt_num(params$toyota_ceiling_km / params$subaru_ceiling_km, 0)`.

That is what makes the comparison worth anything: with the hardware and the contract architecture both held fixed, the mileage ceiling is the only free variable, and the two firms set it two-thirds of an order of magnitude apart.

```{r hv-assumption, include=FALSE}
# If Subaru's service-activated extension did NOT cover the traction battery,
# the Subaru side would fall back to the base term on both axes.
gap_no_hv <- function(rate) {
  map_dbl(names(cal), \(k) gap_value(
    rate, cal[[k]]$a, cal[[k]]$b, cal[[k]]$sd_unit, d_crit,
    params$age_ceiling, params$toyota_ceiling_km,
    subaru_ceiling_km = params$base_km,
    params$severity_buyer_dkk, params$severity_decline, params$discount_real,
    params$repair_worthy, subaru_years = params$base_years
  )$pv_dkk) |>
    set_names(names(cal))
}

hv_mine <- gap_no_hv(my$rate)
hv_median <- gap_no_hv(params$med_rate)
```

> **Load-bearing assumption: the extension covers the traction battery.** Subaru's `r params$age_ceiling`-year / `r fmt_km(params$subaru_ceiling_km)` km service-activated warranty is taken throughout to include the 400 V traction battery at the `r fmt_pct(params$soh_threshold, 0)` capacity threshold, on the terms of the Subaru Norge release of 16 January 2026 (Appendix C). If instead it covered only the rest of the vehicle, the Subaru's battery cover would revert to the base `r params$base_years` yr / `r fmt_km(params$base_km)` km — and the consequence is very unevenly distributed.
>
> At high mileage it barely matters: the mileage ceiling binds long before either age limit, so at `r fmt_km(my$rate)` km/yr the gap would widen only from `r rng(my$gap_full)` to `r rng(hv_mine)` DKK. **Where it matters is at low mileage, and there it is decisive rather than marginal.** Below `r fmt_km(gap_opens_at)` km/yr the contracts are identical *only because* Subaru's battery cover is assumed to run to `r params$age_ceiling` years. Strip that away and the Subaru's cover ends at year `r params$base_years` while the Toyota's runs to `r params$age_ceiling`, opening a gap for every driver however slowly they drive: at the median `r fmt_km(params$med_rate)` km/yr it would be worth `r rng(hv_median)` DKK, against exactly zero as modelled.
>
> So the finding that the two contracts are indistinguishable for most private buyers rests entirely on this one clause. It is the first thing to confirm in the Danish *garantibetingelser*.

> **Unmodelled clause.** Subaru's "no extension granted past `r fmt_km(params$subaru_no_grant_km)` km" is *not* in the model, which treats the Subaru ceiling as a clean `r fmt_km(params$subaru_ceiling_km)` km. The clause restricts when an extension may be *granted*, not how far a granted extension runs, so an owner presenting at `r fmt_km(params$subaru_no_grant_km)` km still reaches `r fmt_km(params$subaru_ceiling_km)` km. It bites only for owners who first present between `r fmt_km(params$subaru_no_grant_km)` and `r fmt_km(params$subaru_ceiling_km)` km. The effect is small and works against Subaru, so every Subaru figure below is mildly generous to Subaru — i.e. the computed contract gap is a **conservative** estimate.

### 2.1 Toyota runs two battery covers, not one

Toyota covers the battery under two separate guarantees, with different terms and different triggers. Only one of them is what this note is about.

```{r two-covers}
tibble(
  Cover = c("**Fejl på batteriet** (defect)", "**Kapacitet på batteriet** (capacity)"),
  `Base term` = c("5 yr / 100,000 km", paste0(params$base_years, " yr / ",
                                              fmt_km(params$base_km), " km")),
  Trigger = c("Battery fault; replaced to at least original capacity",
              paste0("State of health falls below ", fmt_pct(params$soh_threshold, 0))),
  `Extended by health check?` = c("Yes", "Yes")
) |>
  show_table(align = "llll")
```

Both are extended by the same EV health check, at one year or `r fmt_km(params$increment_km)` km per check, to the same `r params$age_ceiling` yr / `r fmt_km(params$toyota_ceiling_km)` km ceiling. **This note models the capacity cover only**, which is the one that differs between the two makes and the one a mileage ceiling is about.

The distinction is worth holding on to when reading other sources. Summaries of Toyota's EV battery warranty in the European press quote either term depending on which cover they have in view, and a description of "5 years / 100,000 km" for this platform is the defect cover rather than a shorter capacity guarantee.

### 2.2 The increment rule is the operative mechanism

Coverage does not extend in years. It extends in **1 year or `r fmt_km(params$increment_km)` km, whichever comes first** — a *rate* limiter, not merely a terminal cap. Coverage accrues at `r fmt_km(params$increment_km)` km per health check regardless of how fast the odometer turns. So the number of dealer visits needed to ride the coverage to any odometer $K$ is

$$n(K) = \frac{K - `r fmt_km(params$base_km)`}{`r fmt_km(params$increment_km)`}$$

```{r checks-table}
tibble(cap_km = c(params$subaru_ceiling_km, 400000, params$toyota_ceiling_km)) |>
  mutate(
    `Target odometer` = c(
      paste0(fmt_km(cap_km[1]), " km (Subaru ceiling)"),
      paste0(fmt_km(cap_km[2]), " km"),
      paste0(fmt_km(cap_km[3]), " km (Toyota ceiling)")
    ),
    `Extra checks` = fmt_num(
      checks_required(cap_km, params$base_km, params$increment_km)
    ),
    `Total checks from zero` = fmt_num(
      checks_required(cap_km, params$base_km, params$increment_km, from_zero = TRUE)
    )
  ) |>
  select(-cap_km) |>
  show_table()
```

The million kilometres is reachable. It costs **`r fmt_num(checks_to_toyota, 0)` trips to a Toyota dealer**, and to do it inside the `r params$age_ceiling`-year age ceiling requires averaging `r fmt_km(params$toyota_ceiling_km / params$age_ceiling)` km/yr — about `r fmt_num(checks_to_toyota / params$age_ceiling)` visits per year for a decade.

---

## 3. Actuarial framework

### 3.1 Two-dimensional warranty region

A warranty of this kind is **two-dimensional**: it expires on whichever of two clocks runs out first, age or odometer. Coverage is therefore the rectangle $\Omega = [0, T] \times [0, K]$ in (age, odometer) space, where $T$ is the age ceiling (`r params$age_ceiling` years) and $K$ the mileage ceiling. A claim is admissible only if *both* coordinates are still inside the rectangle at the moment the battery crosses the threshold.

The notation, since it recurs throughout:

- $X(t)$ is the **odometer reading at age $t$** — cumulative distance driven, the second coordinate of the rectangle. It is modelled as $X(t) = R \cdot t$: constant-rate driving, no seasonality or trend.
- $R$ is the **random usage rate** in km/yr, a property of the *driver*, drawn once when the car is sold and fixed thereafter. It is the only source of cross-sectional variation in how the two clocks race each other.
- $g(r)$ is the **density of $R$** across the buyer population — here lognormal with median `r fmt_km(params$med_rate)` km/yr. Lower-case $r$ is a particular realised value of $R$, i.e. one specific driver's annual mileage.
- $W(r)$ is the **effective warranty term in years** for a driver who does $r$ km/yr.

The last is the object that does the work. For a *given* driver the odometer clock is no longer random — it is a known linear function of age — so the two-dimensional rectangle collapses to a single number, the age at which whichever ceiling binds first is reached:

$$W(r) = \min\left(T, \frac{K}{r}\right)$$

Read directly: a driver reaches the mileage ceiling after $K/r$ years, and the age ceiling after $T$ years, and the warranty ends at the earlier of the two. There is a kink at $r = K/T$. Below that rate the mileage ceiling is never reached inside $T$ years and the contract is purely an age-limited one — the value of $K$ is then completely irrelevant to that buyer. Above it, the mileage ceiling binds strictly first and $T$ becomes irrelevant instead. **This kink is the entire subject of the note**: Toyota and Subaru differ only in $K$, so they differ only for drivers above their respective kinks.

```{r fig-region, fig.height=5.4}
y_max <- params$toyota_ceiling_km * 1.04
rates_ray <- c(15000, 25000, 40000, 60000,
               params$toyota_ceiling_km / params$age_ceiling)

rays <- tibble(r = rates_ray) |>
  mutate(t_end = pmin(params$age_ceiling, y_max / r), x_end = r * t_end)

# Mark an exit only where the MILEAGE ceiling binds; below the kink rate the
# driver leaves on the age axis, not the odometer axis.
exits <- tibble(r = rates_ray) |>
  mutate(
    sub_binds = r > params$subaru_ceiling_km / params$age_ceiling,
    toy_binds = r >= params$toyota_ceiling_km / params$age_ceiling,
    t_sub = params$subaru_ceiling_km / r,
    t_toy = params$toyota_ceiling_km / r
  )

ggplot() +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 0, xmax = params$age_ceiling,
           ymin = params$subaru_ceiling_km, ymax = params$toyota_ceiling_km,
           fill = pal[["toyota"]], alpha = 0.13) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 0, xmax = params$age_ceiling,
           ymin = 0, ymax = params$subaru_ceiling_km,
           fill = pal[["neutral"]], alpha = 0.16) +
  annotate("segment", x = 0, xend = params$age_ceiling,
           y = params$subaru_ceiling_km, yend = params$subaru_ceiling_km,
           colour = pal[["subaru"]], linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("segment", x = 0, xend = params$age_ceiling,
           y = params$toyota_ceiling_km, yend = params$toyota_ceiling_km,
           colour = pal[["toyota"]], linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("segment", x = params$age_ceiling, xend = params$age_ceiling,
           y = 0, yend = params$toyota_ceiling_km,
           colour = "grey40", linewidth = 0.5, linetype = "22") +
  geom_segment(data = rays, aes(x = 0, y = 0, xend = t_end, yend = x_end),
               colour = pal[["neutral"]], linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_point(data = filter(exits, sub_binds),
             aes(x = t_sub, y = params$subaru_ceiling_km),
             colour = pal[["subaru"]], size = 2.1) +
  geom_point(data = filter(exits, toy_binds),
             aes(x = t_toy, y = params$toyota_ceiling_km),
             colour = pal[["toyota"]], size = 2.1) +
  geom_text(data = rays, aes(x = t_end, y = x_end, label = lab_km(r)),
            hjust = -0.12, vjust = 0.4, size = 2.9, colour = pal[["neutral"]]) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.3, y = params$toyota_ceiling_km * 0.66,
           label = "TOYOTA ONLY\nthe contract gap", hjust = 0, size = 3.3,
           colour = pal[["toyota"]], lineheight = 1, fontface = "bold") +
  # Sits under the slowest ray, in the only part of the lower band no ray
  # crosses. The age-ceiling line needs no label: the x axis already reads T.
  annotate("text", x = params$age_ceiling * 0.63,
           y = params$subaru_ceiling_km * 0.22,
           label = "COVERED BY BOTH", hjust = 0, size = 3.1, colour = "grey20",
           fontface = "bold") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = lab_km, expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.02))) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = scales::breaks_width(2),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0.01, 0.10))) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, params$age_ceiling * 1.13), ylim = c(0, y_max)) +
  labs(
    title = "The warranty region, and which drivers reach its edges",
    subtitle = "Cover is the rectangle [0, T] x [0, K]; a driver traces the ray X(t) = r t. Rays labelled in km/yr.",
    x = "Vehicle age (years)", y = "Odometer (km)",
    caption = paste0(
      "Dots mark where the mileage ceiling ends cover: vermillion = Subaru, blue = Toyota. Drivers below\n",
      lab_km(gap_opens_at), " km/yr never enter the upper band, so for them the two contracts are identical. The ",
      lab_km(params$toyota_ceiling_km / params$age_ceiling), " km/yr\n",
      "ray is the only one that reaches Toyota's ceiling inside the age limit, and it arrives exactly at the corner."
    )
  ) +
  theme_note()
```

Expected cost per unit sold then follows by averaging the conditional claim probability over the population of drivers — the classical form for two-dimensional warranties, due to Blischke and Murthy:

$$E[C] = c \int_0^\infty F\!\left(W(r) \mid r\right) g(r)\, dr$$

Here $c$ is the severity (cost per claim) and $F(\cdot \mid r)$ the probability that a driver of type $r$ has crossed the capacity threshold by a given age. So $F(W(r) \mid r)$ is the probability that *this* driver claims before *their* warranty expires, and the integral is its population average. In insurance vocabulary the result is the **pure premium** — the expected claim cost per policy, before any expense or profit margin.

Since $K$ only matters above the kink, the mileage cap can bind only for the fraction of the fleet driving faster than $K/T$. That fraction is worth tabulating, because it turns out to be small:

```{r truncation-table}
# Always show the two contract ceilings and the base, whatever the cap grid is.
trunc_rows <- sort(unique(c(
  params$base_km, params$subaru_ceiling_km, params$toyota_ceiling_km,
  cap_grid[cap_grid > params$base_km & cap_grid < params$toyota_ceiling_km]
)))

tibble(K = trunc_rows) |>
  mutate(
    kink = K / params$age_ceiling,
    share = fleet_truncated(K, params$age_ceiling,
                            params$med_rate, params$sdlog_rate)
  ) |>
  transmute(
    `K (km)` = fmt_km(K),
    `Kink rate K/T (km/yr)` = fmt_km(kink),
    `P(R > K/T)` = fmt_pct(share, 2)
  ) |>
  show_table()
```

```{r truncation-reads, include=FALSE}
# Computed rather than looked up, so the prose survives any cap grid.
trunc_at <- \(k) fleet_truncated(k, params$age_ceiling,
                                 params$med_rate, params$sdlog_rate)

# Mid-range comparator for the non-linearity point: the grid entry closest to
# the geometric midpoint of the two ceilings.
mid_cap <- cap_grid[which.min(abs(
  log(cap_grid) - mean(log(c(params$subaru_ceiling_km, params$toyota_ceiling_km)))
))]
```

**Reading the table.** The middle column is the kink rate: drive faster than this and the mileage ceiling bites before the age ceiling. The right column is the share of the fleet that does.

The base contract's `r fmt_km(params$base_km)` km ceiling constrains `r fmt_pct(trunc_at(params$base_km), 0)` of drivers — a genuinely binding limit for a large share of the fleet, which is what makes the extension mechanism worth having at all. Subaru's `r fmt_km(params$subaru_ceiling_km)` km ceiling still binds for `r fmt_pct(trunc_at(params$subaru_ceiling_km), 0)`: about one buyer in `r fmt_num(1 / trunc_at(params$subaru_ceiling_km), 0)` drives fast enough to hit it inside `r params$age_ceiling` years. Toyota's `r fmt_km(params$toyota_ceiling_km)` km ceiling binds for `r fmt_pct(trunc_at(params$toyota_ceiling_km), 2)` — about one buyer in `r fmt_dkk(1 / trunc_at(params$toyota_ceiling_km))` — since reaching it inside the age ceiling means averaging `r fmt_km(params$toyota_ceiling_km / params$age_ceiling)` km/yr for a decade.

```{r fig-tail, fig.height=4.6}
kinks <- tibble(
  who = c(paste0("Base ", fmt_km(params$base_km), " km"),
          paste0("Subaru ", fmt_km(params$subaru_ceiling_km), " km"),
          paste0("Toyota ", fmt_km(params$toyota_ceiling_km), " km")),
  K = c(params$base_km, params$subaru_ceiling_km, params$toyota_ceiling_km),
  col = c("grey30", pal[["subaru"]], pal[["toyota"]])
) |>
  mutate(
    kink = K / params$age_ceiling,
    share = trunc_at(K)
  )

r_hi <- max(kinks$kink) * 1.18
y_floor <- min(kinks$share) / 3

# Labels sit as a key in the empty upper-right rather than beside their points:
# on a log scale the curve descends through any offset generous enough to clear
# the point itself.
kinks <- kinks |>
  mutate(key_x = r_hi * 0.47,
         key_y = 10^seq(log10(0.85), log10(0.85) - 1.3, length.out = 3))

tibble(r = seq(r_hi * 0.035, r_hi, length.out = 600)) |>
  mutate(share = plnorm(r, log(params$med_rate), params$sdlog_rate,
                        lower.tail = FALSE)) |>
  ggplot(aes(r, share)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.85, colour = pal[["neutral"]]) +
  geom_segment(data = kinks, aes(x = kink, xend = kink, y = y_floor, yend = share),
               colour = kinks$col, linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_point(data = kinks, aes(x = kink, y = share), colour = kinks$col,
             size = 2.5) +
  geom_point(data = kinks, aes(x = key_x, y = key_y), colour = kinks$col,
             size = 2.5) +
  geom_text(data = kinks,
            aes(x = key_x + r_hi * 0.026, y = key_y,
                label = paste0(who, ": ", percent(share, accuracy = 0.01))),
            hjust = 0, colour = kinks$col, size = 2.95) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 0.01),
                limits = c(y_floor, 1.6)) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = lab_km, expand = expansion(mult = c(0.03, 0.04))) +
  labs(
    title = "The share of drivers a mileage ceiling can possibly constrain",
    subtitle = "P(R > K/T): drivers fast enough to reach the ceiling inside the age limit",
    x = "Kink rate K/T (km/yr)", y = "Share of fleet (log scale)",
    caption = paste0(
      "Vertical scale is logarithmic. Raising the ceiling from ",
      lab_km(params$subaru_ceiling_km), " to ", lab_km(params$toyota_ceiling_km),
      " km, a factor of ",
      fmt_num(params$toyota_ceiling_km / params$subaru_ceiling_km, 0),
      ", cuts the constrained\nshare by a factor of about ",
      fmt_num(trunc_at(params$subaru_ceiling_km) / trunc_at(params$toyota_ceiling_km), 0),
      ". The lognormal tail thins far faster than the ceiling rises, which is why the\n",
      "marketing difference between the two numbers and their actuarial difference diverge so sharply."
    )
  ) +
  theme_note()
```

Two things follow, and they set up everything after.

1. **The fall-off is brutally non-linear.** Going from `r fmt_km(params$subaru_ceiling_km)` to `r fmt_km(mid_cap)` km takes the constrained share from `r fmt_pct(trunc_at(params$subaru_ceiling_km), 0)` to `r fmt_pct(trunc_at(mid_cap), 0)`. Going on from `r fmt_km(mid_cap)` to `r fmt_km(params$toyota_ceiling_km)` takes it from `r fmt_pct(trunc_at(mid_cap), 0)` to essentially nothing. This is the lognormal tail thinning out, and it means the *marketing* difference between the two ceilings (a factor of `r fmt_num(params$toyota_ceiling_km / params$subaru_ceiling_km, 0)`) has almost nothing to do with the *population* difference.
2. **This is an upper bound on how much the cap can matter, not an estimate of it.** The table counts drivers who *reach* the ceiling, not drivers who reach it *and* have a degraded battery. The second condition is much rarer, and section 4 shows the two interact: if a pack that is going to fail on throughput fails before the odometer reaches $K$ anyway, then raising $K$ removes no liability at all, however many drivers get there.

### 3.2 Degradation, not hazard

Reliability work usually models failure through a **hazard rate** — the same object as in duration econometrics, the instantaneous exit rate conditional on survival so far — and usually assumes it is Weibull, i.e. a power function of age. That is the wrong instrument here. A hazard describes an event that *strikes* a still-functioning unit at random; a battery warranty claim is not that. Capacity declines smoothly and monotonically, and the claim is triggered when the decline crosses a contractual line. The right object is therefore a **first-passage time** — the age at which a continuously observed process first hits a barrier — which is a deterministic function of the degradation path rather than a random arrival on top of it.

The distinction matters practically, not just semantically. Under a hazard model the mileage and age axes would be roughly interchangeable ways of buying exposure. Under a first-passage model they are not: cumulative distance *drives* the state variable, so the odometer is on the causal path and age is only partly so. That asymmetry is the entire content of section 4.

Capacity loss decomposes into calendar and throughput terms:

$$L(t, x) = Z \left( a\sqrt{t} + b\,x \right), \qquad x = r t$$

The $\sqrt{t}$ calendar term follows from SEI-layer growth; the linear throughput term from cycle count. $Z$ is a unit-level multiplicative heterogeneity factor, lognormal with unit mean, capturing cell-lot and duty-cycle variation.

Setting $L = D_{\text{crit}} = `r d_crit`$ and substituting $u = \sqrt{t}$ gives a quadratic in $u$:

$$b r u^2 + a u - \frac{D_{\text{crit}}}{Z} = 0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
t_{\text{fail}} = \left[\frac{-a + \sqrt{a^2 + 4 b r D_{\text{crit}} / Z}}{2 b r}\right]^{2}$$

**This note does not simulate that root.** Conditional on a fixed usage rate, failure by time $t$ is a statement about $Z$ alone — it occurs iff $Z \ge D_{\text{crit}} / (a\sqrt{t} + b r t)$ — and since $Z$ is lognormal the conditional failure distribution is available in closed form:

$$F(t \mid r) = \Phi\!\left(\frac{\log\left(a\sqrt{t} + b r t\right) - \log D_{\text{crit}} - \sigma^2/2}{\sigma}\right)$$

Everything at the buyer level uses this directly, and fleet-level results mix it over $g(r)$ by numerical integration. This is exact and instant, and it removes Monte Carlo noise — which matters, because calibration A produces gap probabilities down to ~$10^{-4}$, where a million draws is not enough to resolve the answer to the precision the tables report.

Two richer specifications are standard in the degradation literature if the deterministic path above is felt to be too rigid. Both replace "a fixed path scaled by a random factor" with "a genuinely random path". The **gamma process** accumulates strictly positive increments, which is the natural choice for wear that cannot undo itself:

$$P(T_D \le t) = \frac{\Gamma\!\left(\alpha t^{z},\, \beta D_{\text{crit}}\right)}{\Gamma\!\left(\alpha t^{z}\right)}$$

A Wiener process with drift — Brownian motion with a trend, the workhorse of financial modelling — gives the inverse Gaussian first-passage density instead. It is analytically friendlier, but its increments can be negative, which here would mean a pack spontaneously regaining capacity. Neither is used below: the closed form above is exact for the stated model, and the additional process risk would be calibrated on data this note does not have.

### 3.3 Persistency is indexed on distance, not time

**Persistency** is the insurance term for the tendency of a policy to stay in force, and **lapse** for its termination because the holder stopped doing what the contract required — here, missing a health check. It matters because a lapsed policy costs the insurer nothing: expected claims must be multiplied by the probability the cover is still alive when the claim would fall due.

The unusual feature of this contract is what the lapse process is indexed on. A conventional policy lapses when a premium is missed, so persistency runs on the calendar. Here, coverage is extended per health check and checks fall due every `r fmt_km(params$increment_km)` km, so lapse runs on the **odometer**. A high-mileage driver faces the lapse hazard more often per year than a low-mileage one, and — because the ceiling is fixed in kilometres — faces exactly the same number of checks to reach it.

#### Does a missed check destroy the cover, or only suspend it?

Everything about the size of the lapse effect turns on this, and the two readings are worlds apart.

- **Permanent forfeiture.** One missed check ends the cover for good. Survival then decays geometrically in the number of checks, $p(x) = \pi^{\max(0,\ (x - `r fmt_km(params$base_km)`)/`r fmt_km(params$increment_km)`)}$, and over the `r fmt_num(extra_to_toyota, 0)` at-risk checks Toyota's ceiling demands, even high compliance compounds into near-certain loss.
- **Suspension and reinstatement.** A missed check suspends cover until the next completed one, which starts a fresh term. The probability of being covered *when a claim arrives* is then just $\pi$ — the chance the current window's check was done — regardless of how many were missed earlier.

**Toyota Denmark's published terms point to the second.** The battery page says a new guarantee can be activated by a health check *"helt indtil bilen fylder `r params$age_ceiling` år eller har kørt 1 mio km"* — at any point up to the ceiling, not only in unbroken sequence. The Relax conditions are explicit that a missed service *"diskvalificerer dette dig ikke til fremtidig dækning"*, with cover resuming 30 days after the next completed service. The note therefore uses **`r params$lapse_mode`** as its default, and reports both.

```{r persistency-table}
expand_grid(pi_check = c(0.98, 0.95, 0.90),
            mode = c("reinstatable", "permanent")) |>
  mutate(
    sub = map2_dbl(pi_check, mode, \(p, m) coverage_held(
      params$subaru_ceiling_km, p, params$base_km, params$increment_km, m)),
    toy = map2_dbl(pi_check, mode, \(p, m) coverage_held(
      params$toyota_ceiling_km, p, params$base_km, params$increment_km, m))
  ) |>
  transmute(
    `pi per check` = fmt_num(pi_check, 2),
    Regime = mode,
    !!paste0("Covered at ", fmt_km(params$subaru_ceiling_km), " km") := fmt_num(sub, 3),
    !!paste0("Covered at ", fmt_km(params$toyota_ceiling_km), " km") := fmt_num(toy, 3)
  ) |>
  show_table()
```

The contrast is the whole point. Under permanent forfeiture Toyota's ceiling is largely self-defeating — at $\pi = 0.95$ barely `r fmt_pct(coverage_held(params$toyota_ceiling_km, 0.95, params$base_km, params$increment_km, "permanent"), 1)` of owners still hold cover at the million, because the decay compounds over `r fmt_num(extra_to_toyota, 0)` at-risk checks against Subaru's `r fmt_num(extra_to_subaru)`. Under reinstatement the asymmetry vanishes entirely: both makes sit at $\pi$, and the number of checks stops mattering.

> **Which checks are at risk.** Under the permanent reading the $\max(0, \cdot)$ carries more weight than it looks. Counting *all* checks from zero instead would give `r fmt_num(0.98^(params$subaru_ceiling_km / params$increment_km), 3)` and `r fmt_num(0.98^(params$toyota_ceiling_km / params$increment_km), 3)` at $\pi = 0.98$, against `r fmt_num(coverage_held(params$subaru_ceiling_km, 0.98, params$base_km, params$increment_km, "permanent"), 3)` and `r fmt_num(coverage_held(params$toyota_ceiling_km, 0.98, params$base_km, params$increment_km, "permanent"), 3)` — a large difference, and the wrong one. The from-zero count conflates two distinct things: failing a check the contract required, which affects cover, and never having been a dealer-servicing customer in the first place, which does not.

Expected claim cost then carries the lapse factor inside the integral:

$$E[C] = c \int_0^\infty \int_0^{W(r)} p(rt)\, f(t \mid r)\, dt\ g(r)\, dr$$

### 3.4 Competing risks

A **competing risks** setting — the same construction as in duration econometrics — is one where a unit can exit through more than one route and only the first exit is observed. Here there are two: an outright hardware failure (cell short, BMS fault, thermal event), and the gradual capacity decline modelled above. Either triggers a claim, so claim-free survival requires avoiding both:

$$S(t) = \exp\left(-\int_0^t h_{\text{hard}}(u)\,du\right) \cdot P\!\left(D(t) < D_{\text{crit}}\right)$$

$S(t)$ is the survival function — the probability of reaching age $t$ with no claim of either kind. It is written $S$ rather than the conventional $R$ for reliability to avoid colliding with the usage rate $R$ of section 3.1.

The hard-failure leg is Weibull with shape $\beta < 1$, meaning a hazard that *falls* with age — **infant mortality**, where manufacturing defects surface early and a unit that survives its first years is safer than a new one.

Toyota's Danish terms give this leg its own contract: the *"Fejl på batteriet"* cover of 5 yr / 100,000 km (section 2.1), which is shorter than the capacity cover rather than co-extensive with it. That does not change the conclusion. Infant-mortality failures land overwhelmingly inside the first years; the defect cover is extended by the same health check on the same terms; and Subaru's arrangement is structurally alike. The hard-failure leg therefore still cannot differentiate the two contracts, and is dropped from everything below. Only the degradation leg is modelled — but the reason is the shape of the hazard, not the length of the term.

---

## 4. The central result: when does a mileage cap bind?

Define $x_{\text{crit}}$ as the odometer at which the degradation path crosses the threshold. Because loss is monotone in cumulative throughput, a vehicle claims at approximately $x_{\text{crit}}$ regardless of how fast it got there, once the throughput term dominates the calendar term. Hence:

$$\boxed{K \text{ binds} \iff K < x_{\text{crit}}}$$

```{r xcrit}
tibble(calib = names(cal)) |>
  transmute(
    Calibration = map_chr(calib, \(k) cal[[k]]$label),
    `x_crit (km)` = map_chr(calib, \(k) fmt_km(round(
      x_crit(cal[[k]]$calendar_loss_10y, cal[[k]]$km_crit_pure, d_crit)
    ))),
    `Toyota ceiling binds?` = map_chr(calib, \(k) ifelse(
      params$toyota_ceiling_km <
        x_crit(cal[[k]]$calendar_loss_10y, cal[[k]]$km_crit_pure, d_crit),
      "yes", "no"
    )),
    `Subaru ceiling binds?` = map_chr(calib, \(k) ifelse(
      params$subaru_ceiling_km <
        x_crit(cal[[k]]$calendar_loss_10y, cal[[k]]$km_crit_pure, d_crit),
      "yes", "no"
    ))
  ) |>
  show_table()
```

```{r fig-xcrit, fig.width=8.2, fig.height=5}
# Must contain ref_rate, or the highlighted median path and its heterogeneity
# band silently drop out of the figure while the caption still describes them.
rates_deg <- sort(unique(c(
  params$med_rate, params$ref_rate, buyer_rates[buyer_rates > gap_opens_at]
)))
stopifnot(params$ref_rate %in% rates_deg)

x_seq <- seq(1000, params$toyota_ceiling_km * 1.02, length.out = 500)

deg <- expand_grid(calib = names(cal), r = rates_deg, x = x_seq) |>
  mutate(
    a = map_dbl(calib, \(k) cal[[k]]$a),
    b = map_dbl(calib, \(k) cal[[k]]$b),
    sd_unit = map_dbl(calib, \(k) cal[[k]]$sd_unit),
    path = a * sqrt(x / r) + b * x,
    med = path * exp(-sd_unit^2 / 2),
    lab = map_chr(calib, \(k) cal[[k]]$label)
  )

band <- deg |>
  filter(r == params$ref_rate) |>
  mutate(
    lo = path * qlnorm(0.10, -sd_unit^2 / 2, sd_unit),
    hi = path * qlnorm(0.90, -sd_unit^2 / 2, sd_unit)
  )

xcrit_tbl <- tibble(calib = names(cal)) |>
  mutate(
    lab = map_chr(calib, \(k) cal[[k]]$label),
    xc = map_dbl(calib, \(k) x_crit(cal[[k]]$calendar_loss_10y,
                                    cal[[k]]$km_crit_pure, d_crit))
  )

y_top <- d_crit * 1.5

ggplot(deg, aes(x, med)) +
  geom_ribbon(data = band, aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = pal[["neutral"]],
              alpha = 0.16) +
  geom_vline(data = xcrit_tbl, aes(xintercept = xc), colour = "grey45",
             linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = params$subaru_ceiling_km, colour = pal[["subaru"]],
             linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = params$toyota_ceiling_km, colour = pal[["toyota"]],
             linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = d_crit, linetype = "22", colour = "grey15",
             linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_line(aes(group = r), colour = pal[["neutral"]], linewidth = 0.45,
            alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_line(data = band, aes(x, med), colour = "black", linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_text(data = xcrit_tbl, aes(x = xc, y = y_top * 0.955, label = "x_crit"),
            hjust = 1.15, size = 2.9, colour = "grey40") +
  annotate("text", x = params$subaru_ceiling_km, y = y_top * 0.955,
           label = "Subaru ", hjust = 1, size = 2.9, colour = pal[["subaru"]]) +
  annotate("text", x = params$toyota_ceiling_km, y = y_top * 0.955,
           label = " Toyota", hjust = 1.05, size = 2.9, colour = pal[["toyota"]]) +
  annotate("text", x = params$toyota_ceiling_km * 0.02, y = d_crit,
           label = "claim threshold", vjust = -0.65, hjust = 0, size = 2.9,
           colour = "grey15") +
  facet_wrap(~lab) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_comma(scale = 1e-3, suffix = "k"),
                     breaks = scales::breaks_width(params$toyota_ceiling_km / 4)) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, y_top)) +
  labs(
    title = "A mileage ceiling binds only if it sits below x_crit",
    subtitle = paste0("Capacity loss against odometer, for drivers at ",
                      lab_km(min(rates_deg)), " to ", lab_km(max(rates_deg)), " km/yr"),
    x = "Odometer (km)", y = "Capacity loss (percentage points)",
    caption = paste0(
      "Thin grey lines: median path at each usage rate. They nearly coincide, so a pack crosses the threshold at\n",
      "roughly the same odometer however fast it got there. Bold line and band: median and 10th to 90th percentile\n",
      "of unit heterogeneity Z at ", lab_km(params$ref_rate), " km/yr. Subaru's ceiling cuts through the paths well before they cross;\n",
      "Toyota's sits beyond the point where every throughput-driven claim has already happened, so it censors nothing."
    )
  ) +
  theme_note()
```

Above $x_{\text{crit}}$ the cap is not a weak constraint — it is a **null** constraint. Every vehicle that would ever claim on throughput has already claimed before reaching the cap. The mileage axis stops being a liability limiter the moment it exceeds the pack's own throughput life.

Toyota placed their ceiling above $x_{\text{crit}}$ on both calibrations; Subaru placed theirs well below on both.

---

## 5. Calibration

The degradation model has no published fade curve to fit, so it is run under two bracketing scenarios rather than one central estimate. The bottom row is the **claim rate**: expected claims per vehicle sold, which — since a pack is replaced at most once here — is also the probability that a given vehicle ever claims. "Uncapped" means with the mileage ceiling removed entirely, leaving only the `r params$age_ceiling`-year age limit, so it measures the degradation model alone before any contract geometry is applied.

```{r calibration-table}
tibble(calib = names(cal)) |>
  mutate(
    cc = map(calib, \(k) cal[[k]]),
    `Calendar loss at 10 yr` = map_chr(cc, \(c) paste0(c$calendar_loss_10y, "%")),
    `x_crit (pure throughput)` = map_chr(cc, \(c) paste0(
      fmt_km(round(x_crit(c$calendar_loss_10y, c$km_crit_pure, d_crit))), " km"
    )),
    `Unit heterogeneity sigma` = map_chr(cc, \(c) fmt_num(c$sd_unit, 2)),
    `Median loss at 10 yr / 150,000 km` = map_chr(cc, \(c) paste0(
      fmt_num(loss_path(10, 15000, c$a, c$b) * exp(-c$sd_unit^2 / 2)), "%"
    )),
    `Uncapped 10-yr claim rate` = map_chr(calib, \(k) fmt_pct(uncapped[[k]], 2))
  ) |>
  transmute(Quantity = map_chr(cc, \(c) c$label),
            `Calendar loss at 10 yr`, `x_crit (pure throughput)`,
            `Unit heterogeneity sigma`, `Median loss at 10 yr / 150,000 km`,
            `Uncapped 10-yr claim rate`) |>
  pivot_longer(-Quantity, names_to = "Parameter") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = Quantity, values_from = value) |>
  show_table(align = "lrr")
```

A approximates Toyota's stated engineering aspiration; B represents a fast-fade fleet. The spread between them is the dominant uncertainty in everything below.

---

## 6. Fleet-level results

This section takes the manufacturer's view: what the contract costs across everyone who buys the car. Section 7 takes the buyer's.

### 6.1 Retained liability by mileage cap (full compliance, T = `r params$age_ceiling`)

Two columns need defining. **Claim rate** is the expected number of claims per vehicle sold — since a pack is replaced at most once here, it is also the probability that a given vehicle claims. **Retained** is that claim rate as a fraction of the claim rate under no mileage cap at all: the share of the underlying liability the manufacturer still carries after the cap does its work. Retained = 1 means the cap removes nothing; retained = 0 means it removes everything.

```{r cap-table}
cap_table <- tibble(cap_km = cap_grid) |>
  mutate(
    truncated = fleet_truncated(cap_km, params$age_ceiling,
                                params$med_rate, params$sdlog_rate),
    claims_a = map_dbl(cap_km, \(k) rate_of(cal$A, params$age_ceiling, k)),
    claims_b = map_dbl(cap_km, \(k) rate_of(cal$B, params$age_ceiling, k)),
    retained_a = claims_a / uncapped[["A"]],
    retained_b = claims_b / uncapped[["B"]]
  )

cap_table |>
  transmute(
    `K (km)` = fmt_km(cap_km),
    `Fleet truncated` = fmt_pct(truncated, 1),
    `Claim rate A` = fmt_pct(claims_a, 3),
    `Retained A` = fmt_num(retained_a, 3),
    `Claim rate B` = fmt_pct(claims_b, 3),
    `Retained B` = fmt_num(retained_b, 3)
  ) |>
  show_table()
```

```{r leverage, include=FALSE}
lev <- cap_table |>
  filter(truncated > 0, retained_a < 1) |>
  mutate(leverage_a = (1 - retained_a) / truncated) |>
  arrange(desc(leverage_a))
lev_peak <- lev$cap_km[1]
# Two highest-leverage caps, reported low-to-high on both axes so the prose
# ranges read in ascending order.
lev_top <- lev |>
  slice_head(n = 2) |>
  mutate(leverage = (1 - retained_a) / truncated) |>
  arrange(leverage)

sub_row <- cap_table |> filter(cap_km == params$subaru_ceiling_km)
mid_row <- cap_table |> filter(cap_km == 400000)
```

**Leverage effect.** The cap does not sample the fleet at random. At `r fmt_km(params$subaru_ceiling_km)` km it excludes `r fmt_pct(sub_row$truncated, 0)` of vehicles and removes `r fmt_pct(1 - sub_row$retained_b, 1)`–`r fmt_pct(1 - sub_row$retained_a, 1)` of expected claims; at `r fmt_km(400000)` km it excludes `r fmt_pct(mid_row$truncated, 0)` and removes `r fmt_pct(1 - mid_row$retained_b, 0)`–`r fmt_pct(1 - mid_row$retained_a, 0)`. Liability removed per customer disadvantaged peaks around `r fmt_km(min(lev_top$cap_km))`–`r fmt_km(max(lev_top$cap_km))` km, at roughly `r fmt_num(lev_top$leverage[1], 0)`–`r fmt_num(lev_top$leverage[2], 0)`x in calibration A. Both manufacturers sit at corners rather than at that peak, which indicates the cap is not set by an actuarial optimisation.

```{r fig-leverage, fig.height=6.2}
k_grid <- round(exp(seq(log(params$base_km), log(params$toyota_ceiling_km),
                        length.out = 45)))

liab <- expand_grid(calib = names(cal), K = k_grid) |>
  mutate(
    claims = map2_dbl(calib, K, \(k, kk) rate_of(cal[[k]], params$age_ceiling, kk)),
    retained = claims / uncapped[calib],
    truncated = trunc_at(K),
    leverage = (1 - retained) / truncated,
    series = map_chr(calib, \(k) cal[[k]]$label)
  )

p_top <- "Share of liability retained, and share of fleet constrained"
p_bot <- "Liability removed per constrained customer (ratio)"

bind_rows(
  liab |> transmute(K, value = retained, series, panel = p_top),
  liab |> filter(calib == "A") |>
    transmute(K, value = truncated, series = "Fleet constrained by the cap",
              panel = p_top),
  liab |> transmute(K, value = leverage, series, panel = p_bot)
) |>
  mutate(panel = factor(panel, levels = c(p_top, p_bot))) |>
  ggplot(aes(K, value, colour = series)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = params$subaru_ceiling_km, colour = pal[["subaru"]],
             linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = params$toyota_ceiling_km, colour = pal[["toyota"]],
             linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.85) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_log10(labels = lab_km,
                breaks = c(2e5, 3e5, 5e5, 7e5, 1e6)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = setNames(
    c(pal[["A"]], pal[["B"]], "grey45"),
    c(cal$A$label, cal$B$label, "Fleet constrained by the cap")
  )) +
  labs(
    title = "A mileage cap does not sample the fleet at random",
    subtitle = "Dashed verticals mark where the two makers actually set their ceilings",
    x = "Mileage ceiling K (km, log scale)", y = NULL,
    caption = paste0(
      "Top: the share of underlying liability the maker still carries after the cap, against the share of drivers\n",
      "the cap constrains. At Subaru's ", lab_km(params$subaru_ceiling_km),
      " km the cap disadvantages ", fmt_pct(sub_row$truncated, 0),
      " of buyers and removes ",
      fmt_pct(1 - sub_row$retained_b, 1), "-", fmt_pct(1 - sub_row$retained_a, 1), " of\n",
      "expected claims. Bottom: that ratio peaks near ", lab_km(lev_peak),
      " km, at roughly ", fmt_num(max(lev_top$leverage), 0),
      "x on the benign calibration.\n",
      "Both makers sit at a corner rather than at that peak."
    )
  ) +
  theme_note() +
  theme(legend.text = element_text(size = 8.5))
```

### 6.2 With distance-indexed lapse

```{r lapse-table}
lapse_table <- expand_grid(
  calib = names(cal),
  pi_check = pi_grid,
  mode = c("reinstatable", "permanent")
) |>
  mutate(
    sub = pmap_dbl(list(calib, pi_check, mode),
                   \(k, p, m) rate_of(cal[[k]], params$age_ceiling,
                                      params$subaru_ceiling_km, p, m)),
    toy = pmap_dbl(list(calib, pi_check, mode),
                   \(k, p, m) rate_of(cal[[k]], params$age_ceiling,
                                      params$toyota_ceiling_km, p, m)),
    ratio = toy / sub
  ) |>
  # At full compliance the two regimes coincide, so show that row once.
  filter(pi_check < 1 | mode == params$lapse_mode)

lapse_table |>
  transmute(
    Calibration = calib,
    pi = fmt_num(pi_check, 2),
    Regime = ifelse(pi_check >= 1, "—", mode),
    !!paste0(params$age_ceiling, " yr / ",
             fmt_km(params$subaru_ceiling_km), " km") := fmt_pct(sub, 3),
    !!paste0(params$age_ceiling, " yr / ",
             fmt_km(params$toyota_ceiling_km), " km") := fmt_pct(toy, 3),
    # A ratio of 8.5 must not print as "8"; large ones do not need decimals.
    # formatC() does not vectorise over `digits`, hence map2_chr().
    Ratio = paste0(
      map2_chr(ratio, ifelse(ratio >= 100, 0, 1), \(x, d) fmt_num(x, d)), "x"
    )
  ) |>
  show_table()
```

```{r lapse-effect, include=FALSE}
cut_at <- function(m) {
  full <- lapse_table |> filter(calib == "A", pi_check == 1)
  low <- lapse_table |> filter(calib == "A", pi_check == min(pi_grid), mode == m)
  1 - low$toy / full$toy
}
cut_perm <- cut_at("permanent")
cut_rein <- cut_at("reinstatable")
```

**Which regime holds decides whether this section matters at all.** Under permanent forfeiture, lapse cuts Toyota's exposure by roughly `r fmt_pct(cut_perm, 0)` at $\pi = `r fmt_num(min(pi_grid), 2)`$ while barely touching Subaru's, because the geometric decay compounds over `r fmt_num(extra_to_toyota, 0)` at-risk checks rather than `r fmt_num(extra_to_subaru)`. On that reading Toyota's higher ceiling is substantially self-neutralising — the same rule that makes the million reachable also makes it improbable that anyone arrives there with unbroken cover.

Under reinstatement, which is what Toyota Denmark's terms appear to describe (section 3.3), the same compliance rate cuts exposure by only `r fmt_pct(cut_rein, 0)`, and it cuts both makes about equally. **The self-neutralising argument then largely disappears**: Toyota's ceiling is worth close to its full face value, and the number of checks required stops being a defence. This is the single largest correction the Danish terms make to the note, and it runs in Toyota's favour.

The buyer-level sections use full compliance throughout, so they are unaffected either way; a buyer choosing to hold the cover is by construction one who turns up for the checks.

### 6.3 Decomposition of the contract gap (full compliance)

```{r decomposition}
decomp <- tibble(calib = names(cal)) |>
  mutate(
    base = map_dbl(calib, \(k) rate_of(cal[[k]], params$base_years, params$base_km)),
    mile_end = map_dbl(calib, \(k) rate_of(cal[[k]], params$base_years,
                                           params$toyota_ceiling_km)),
    full = map_dbl(calib, \(k) rate_of(cal[[k]], params$age_ceiling,
                                       params$toyota_ceiling_km)),
    mileage_axis = mile_end - base,
    time_axis = full - mile_end,
    total = full - base
  )

tibble(
  Component = c(
    paste0("Mileage axis (", fmt_km(params$base_km), " -> ",
           fmt_km(params$toyota_ceiling_km), ", at ", params$base_years, " yr)"),
    paste0("Time axis (", params$base_years, " -> ", params$age_ceiling,
           " yr, at ", fmt_km(params$toyota_ceiling_km), " km)"),
    paste0("**Total (", params$base_years, "y/", fmt_km(params$base_km), " -> ",
           params$age_ceiling, "y/", fmt_km(params$toyota_ceiling_km), ")**")
  ),
  A = c(
    paste0("+", fmt_num(100 * decomp$mileage_axis[1], 3), " pp"),
    paste0("+", fmt_num(100 * decomp$time_axis[1], 3), " pp"),
    paste0("**+", fmt_num(100 * decomp$total[1], 2), " pp**")
  ),
  B = c(
    paste0("+", fmt_num(100 * decomp$mileage_axis[2], 3), " pp"),
    paste0("+", fmt_num(100 * decomp$time_axis[2], 3), " pp"),
    paste0("**+", fmt_num(100 * decomp$total[2], 2), " pp**")
  )
) |>
  show_table(align = "lrr")
```

```{r extraction, include=FALSE}
# What the top-mileage buyer extracts, per DKK of pooled accrual, on each
# calibration. Reported as a sorted range rather than A-then-B: which
# calibration gives the larger multiple depends on the parameters.
extraction_ratio <- c(
```
